explainers.title: The yield curve and why inversions worry markets
explainers.dek: A simple line linking short-term and long-term interest rates has an uncanny record of warning about recessions. Then came 2022-24, when it sounded the alarm and the US economy kept growing.

spotlights.title: Brazil: the farm to the world with a fragile wallet
spotlights.dek: Brazil feeds much of the planet and sits on vast reserves of oil and iron ore, yet it has struggled for decades with inflation, high interest rates and deep inequality.

explainers.title: How central banks set interest rates
explainers.dek: A committee meets, a number changes by a quarter of a percentage point, and the effects ripple through the economy for up to two years. Here is how that works, and why it is so slow.

spotlights.title: India: a services giant searching for factory jobs
spotlights.dek: The world's most populous country is also its fastest-growing large economy. The question is whether that growth can create enough good jobs for hundreds of millions of young people.

explainers.title: GDP: what it counts and what it misses
explainers.dek: Gross domestic product is the most quoted number in economics. It is brilliant at what it was built to do, and silent on much of what makes life worth living.

spotlights.title: Japan: the economy that lived the future first
spotlights.dek: Deflation, a shrinking population and enormous public debt were once seen as Japan's peculiar problems. Increasingly, they look like a preview of what other rich countries face.

explainers.title: How inflation is measured
explainers.dek: Behind every headline inflation figure sits a basket of hundreds of items, thousands of price checks and a surprising number of judgement calls. Here is how it works.

spotlights.title: Germany: the workshop of Europe at a crossroads
spotlights.dek: Europe's largest economy built its prosperity on cars, machines and cheap energy. Now all three pillars are being tested at once.

explainers.title: Keynesian economics
explainers.dek: Born in the wreckage of the Great Depression, John Maynard Keynes's ideas about spending, saving and unemployment shaped the post-war world, fell from favour, and came roaring back in 2008 and 2020.

spotlights.title: Saudi Arabia: an oil kingdom racing to reinvent itself
spotlights.dek: The world's most important oil exporter is spending heavily to build an economy that can thrive after oil. The ambition is huge; so are the risks.

explainers.title: Monetarism and Milton Friedman
explainers.dek: Milton Friedman convinced a generation that money matters and that inflation is a choice. His ideas tamed the 1970s, then hit trouble in practice. What survives today?

spotlights.title: Nigeria: Africa's giant takes the hard medicine
spotlights.dek: Africa's most populous nation is living through painful reforms to its currency and fuel prices. The bet is that short-term pain will unlock the potential of a young, entrepreneurial population.

explainers.title: Neoliberalism: ideas, history and critiques
explainers.dek: Few words in economics carry so much baggage. What did the thinkers behind neoliberalism actually argue, what happened when governments tried it, and why is the label itself so fiercely disputed?

spotlights.title: South Korea: the miracle economy and its demographic cliff
spotlights.dek: In two generations, South Korea went from war-torn poverty to chip superpower. Now it faces the lowest birth rate on earth and a tightening squeeze between America and China.

explainers.title: Comparative advantage and the case for trade
explainers.dek: Why two countries can both gain from trade even when one is better at everything, and why the people who lose out are real all the same.

spotlights.title: China: the great factory searches for a new engine
spotlights.dek: Four decades of breakneck, investment-led growth made China a manufacturing superpower. Now a property bust, an ageing population and trade friction are forcing a rethink.

explainers.title: Reading the labour market: unemployment, participation and the Phillips curve
explainers.dek: The unemployment rate is the most watched number in economics, but on its own it tells you surprisingly little. Here is how to read the rest of the picture.

spotlights.title: Mexico: America's factory next door
spotlights.dek: Mexico has wired itself into the US economy more tightly than any other country. That brings factories, jobs and remittances, and an uncomfortable dependence on Washington.

explainers.title: Government debt and deficits: when does debt become a problem?
explainers.dek: Japan owes more than twice its annual output and borrows cheaply; Greece owed less and lost market access. The difference lies in arithmetic, currency and trust.

spotlights.title: Norway: how to get rich from oil without spending it
spotlights.dek: Norway struck oil in 1969 and chose to save rather than splurge. Its giant sovereign wealth fund is the envy of the world, but the hardest choices may still lie ahead.

explainers.title: What moves exchange rates
explainers.dek: Interest rates, inflation, trade, fear and the occasional central bank all push currencies around. Here is how to make sense of the world's biggest market.

spotlights.title: Australia: the lucky country digs deep
spotlights.dek: Australia dug its way to prosperity, selling iron ore and coal to Asia and going almost three decades without a recession. Housing costs, China and the energy transition now test its luck.

explainers.title: Quantitative easing explained
explainers.dek: When interest rates hit zero, central banks started buying bonds by the hundreds of billions. What did that actually do, who gained, and what happens now it is being unwound?

spotlights.title: Turkey: a dynamic economy on a monetary rollercoaster
spotlights.dek: Turkey has factories that supply Europe, beaches that draw tens of millions of visitors and a strategic location few can match. Its experiment with unorthodox monetary policy shows how fast inflation can spiral.

explainers.title: Modern Monetary Theory: claims and critiques
explainers.dek: MMT says governments that issue their own currency face an inflation limit, not a money limit. Its supporters call it realism; its critics call it a recipe for trouble.

spotlights.title: Indonesia: the archipelago that wants to make, not just mine
spotlights.dek: The world's fourth most populous country grows steadily on domestic spending and natural resources. Its bold bet on processing nickel at home is reshaping global battery supply chains.

explainers.title: Productivity: why it matters most in the long run
explainers.dek: How much we produce for each hour we work decides, more than anything else, how rich we become. So why has Britain's productivity barely grown since 2008?

spotlights.title: Argentina: breaking the boom-bust cycle with a chainsaw
spotlights.dek: Once among the richest countries on earth, Argentina became a byword for default and inflation. Javier Milei's radical experiment is the latest attempt to escape that history.
